Following a resurgence of 8GB RAM laptops earlier this year , and in the wake of promises to improve Windows 11 performance using just 8GB of RAM , Microsoft has today announced what it claims are a series of performance improvements. Driven by an ongoing global PC component shortage that is forcing manufacturers to dumb down specs, the company says that with 8GB of RAM, Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster when it comes to multitasking.
The development shared today by Microsoft is an update to a commitment earlier this year to improve the quality and performance of Windows 11 , a major bugbear of users since its launch. Microsoft says it has taken a three-pronged approach to memory optimization: making better use of memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting interactions that need to feel instant, and ensuring key apps and Windows use less memory. While the company admits you'll be able to do more on 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it says "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."
The headline performance gain is a claim that Windows is now up to 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs. Likewise, multitasking is now purportedly 40% faster in Microsoft's lab tests. Of course, these are internal tests conducted in favorable conditions by Microsoft.
Microsoft says it has tuned compression for useful apps and data, and can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory, rather than moving it to storage. In practice, this should mean that apps and tabs left open should be less likely to reload when you go back to them.
The claim of 20% more responsiveness specifically relates to tasks like opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, using the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. The company says it has achieved this by backing off background tasks like indexing while you're using your PC actively. Edge now reportedly opens up to 33% faster. There's also an Efficiency Mode for Microsoft Teams, which can be set to on by default, improving launch times by 20%.
Microsoft says that its claims of 40% speed boosts to multitasking are based on a demanding workflow of 20 Microsoft Edge Tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer all being opened one after the other.
Other improvements include reducing committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB in apps like Microsoft Edge and 365 apps, and reducing the memory footprint of Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook by 360MB. Third-party apps can also benefit from improved memory management, with Microsoft stating WhatsApp is already taking advantage.

Moving forward, Microsoft says it has plans to make memory compression even smarter and more efficient. Windows features and apps will share common parts, such as Search and Widgets using one web Engine, for instance. WinUI 3 apps like File Explorer and Notepad will be designed to use less memory and open faster, and Microsoft is working with PC makers and silicon manufacturers to reduce how much memory a PC needs to hold in reserve to support its hardware, making more space for Windows.

articles.title_orig: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.title_zh: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.content_orig:
More than 50 people are feared to be trapped under the rubble
Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.
At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.
He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".
Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.
The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.
Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.
Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof  collapsed, trapping many underneath.
"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.
However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.
The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.
According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.
But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law" , external .
Dozens of terminally ill patients had to evacuate their hospice after it was hit
Further north, in Dnipro, nearly 50 terminally ill patients were being transferred to other facilities after their hospice was destroyed by a Russian missile on Monday night. The oldest of the patients was 90 years old.
Mayor Boris Filatov posted photos on Telegram showing elderly people lying in their beds in a hospice room with blown-out windows and rubble and broken glass strewn on the floors.
Last month, the UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine were at a 'record level'
"I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad.
"These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."
Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.
Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating.
The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".
As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.
It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.
Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.
Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.
US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting. , external
The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities.
At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.
In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

articles.title_orig: Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
articles.title_zh: Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s main opposition leaders have agreed to back former military chief Gadi Eisenkot as prime minister, promising to replace Benjamin Netanyahu’s government as quickly as possible.
The leaders of the Jewish-led opposition alliance met on Tuesday in the city of Herzliya, north of Tel Aviv, in their first joint meeting since the October 27 election , which left neither bloc with a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The agreement comes a day before President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with parties on who should form the next government.
But the bloc remains divided over whether to ally with Arab-led parties, whose support could prove decisive.
In a joint statement, the leaders said all their parties would recommend Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, to Herzog, and that negotiating teams would immediately begin drafting policy guidelines and coalition agreements.
“The party leaders are coordinated and will act immediately” to replace Netanyahu’s coalition “with a national emergency government,” the statement said.
The meeting brought together Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman, Yair Golan of the Democrats, and Yair Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party, according to The Jerusalem Post.
The leaders stood by four principles set out by Eisenkot, including that all parties in government recognise Israel as a Jewish state and label Hamas a “terrorist” group, conditions that could exclude some Arab-led parties.
“We don’t have time – we must act with great urgency,” Bennett, whose party came third, told reporters.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, the opposition 48, and Arab-led parties 19, with the Joint List taking 11 and Ra’am eight. A majority requires 61 seats.
Yousef Jabareen, head of the largest Arab-led party in the next parliament, said the opposition needed to accept “political reality” and join forces to remove Netanyahu.
Golan is the only opposition leader openly backing an alliance with Arab-led parties, saying it is racist to exclude them.
He met the leaders of Arab-led parties before the talks and promised to tackle high crime faced by Palestinian citizens of Israel in their communities.
Afterwards, the two sides stressed their “shared interest in using the parliamentary majority to bring down the Netanyahu-Ben-Gvir-Smotrich government and replace it”, according to a statement.
Liberman has firmly opposed including Arab-led parties, although he also wants to avoid another election.
Israel’s minority Palestinian population has long been marginalised in politics, and even more so since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7 and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
At least two former Palestinian politicians and one current member of the Knesset have been arrested briefly for comments or acts deemed critical of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.
Palestinian citizens of Israel are descendants of Palestinians who managed to remain within the borders of the newly established Israeli state in 1948 after the Nakba , or catastrophe. They make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population.
On Monday, Netanyahu called for a “broad national government” under his leadership, saying his Likud party, with 27 seats, remained the largest. No opposition leader has expressed openness to joining him.
He has ruled out a coalition with the Arab-majority lists, alleging they “support terrorism and deny the existence of the Jewish state”.
Netanyahu, 77, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is on trial on corruption charges and is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in the enclave since Israel began its war in October 2023.
Herzog will hold consultations on Wednesday and Thursday. Eisenkot could receive the most recommendations if he secures the backing of lawmakers from the Arab parties.

articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war.
“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”.
“I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said.
Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons.
On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported.
The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks.
Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”.
He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?”
“There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said.
European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi.
Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year.
Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition.
But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”.
“The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said.
He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 .
Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin.
The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
Cop30 host sets out steps to break link with coal, oil and gas as it aims to move focus from negotiating to implementing
All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference , set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta , Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans , including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
after newsletter promotion
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide , so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the Tropical Forest Forever Facility , a fund aiming to preserve forests, which raised about $7bn from various countries including a £400m loan from the UK.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

articles.title_orig: Ben Saul Attempts to Whitewash $150,000 from China
articles.title_zh: Ben Saul Attempts to Whitewash $150,000 from China
articles.content_orig:
At an October 22, 2026 UN press conference , Ben Saul, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights while countering terrorism, was questioned about his ties to China. The questions followed a UN Watch report revealing that China had contributed $150,000 to his mandate in 2024, as documented in the UN’s 2024 Special Procedures Facts & Figures report , as well as allegations concerning his close personal ties to a Chinese Communist Party official.
Saul’s claims in response raise several questions which are examined below:
Rebuttal: Saul initially suggested that China’s $150,000 contribution was part of its ordinary funding of the United Nations. He emphasized that China is “the second largest contributor to the United Nations budget,” adding that “of course” it funds “United Nations mechanisms, including the human rights system.” He also described the funds as “an allocation which goes to the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva.”
However, the $150,000 did not come from China’s assessed contributions to the UN regular budget. It was a separate, voluntary contribution specifically earmarked for Saul’s mandate.
Moreover, Saul subsequently contradicted his own suggestion that China’s contribution was part of its ordinary UN funding, asserting that his “mandate and many others get no UN regular budget funding.” Not only did this undercut his earlier explanation, but the assertion itself was false. As OHCHR’s own website makes clear, Special Procedures mandates do receive support from the UN regular budget for various activities, including travel to Geneva and New York to present reports to the Human Rights Council and General Assembly, participation in annual meetings, country visits, and other mandated activities.
This regular-budget support is provided through the UN system and is not separately reported as voluntary contributions in the annual Special Procedures Facts & Figures reports .
Thus, Saul’s explanation was misleading in two respects. First, by invoking China’s status as a major contributor to the UN budget, he obscured the distinction between its mandatory contributions and its separate, earmarked funding of his mandate. Second, his categorical assertion that his mandate receives “no UN regular budget funding” ignored the regular-budget support that OHCHR itself identifies as available to Special Procedures.
Rebuttal: Saul portrayed China’s contribution as entirely routine, stating that “there is nothing unusual or untoward about that” and noting that his “mandate also gets some contributions from Spain and Switzerland.”
It is true that Special Procedures mandates rely in part on voluntary contributions from Member States. As OHCHR explains , the UN’s regular budget is insufficient to cover all mandate activities, making additional voluntary contributions necessary under the current system.
OHCHR further states that these contributions are “received by OHCHR,” are “strictly governed by UN financial rules, policies and oversight mechanisms,” and “do not give donors any role in the appointment, direction, priorities, findings or conclusions of mandate holders.” This is consistent with Saul’s assertion that the Chinese funds were channeled through OHCHR in Geneva and that China has no direct control over their expenditure.
However, the fact that voluntary contributions are permitted under UN rules does not mean that China’s contribution to Saul’s mandate was routine.
First , China is not among OHCHR’s leading voluntary contributors. In 2024, China contributed $4 million in voluntary funding, ranking 18th among donors. Yet despite its relatively modest overall contributions, China chose to earmark $150,000 specifically for Saul’s mandate.
Second , China’s contribution was earmarked for Saul’s particular mandate rather than provided as general support for the Special Procedures system. OHCHR distinguishes between earmarked and unearmarked voluntary contributions. Significantly, in Resolution 16/21 , the Human Rights Council welcomed additional voluntary contributions while expressly emphasizing that such contributions should be, to the extent possible, unearmarked.
Third , China’s earmarked funding of Special Procedures has been highly selective. According to UN Watch’s Special Procedures Funding Database , between 2017 and 2025, China contributed a total of $2,249,979 in earmarked funding to just seven of the more than 55 Special Procedures mandates.
Felipe Gonzalez Morales, 2022
The pattern of funding is noteworthy. China has directed substantial earmarked contributions to a small group of mandates, including several whose work impacts China’s domestic issues and foreign policy positions. Most notably, more than $1 million went to the Special Rapporteur on unilateral coercive measures, a mandate focused on condemning sanctions and other measures imposed by Western governments.
Ben Saul is also the only Special Rapporteur on human rights while countering terrorism identified in the database as having received earmarked funding from China.
Saul’s observation that Spain and Switzerland also contribute to his mandate does not address the central issue. China is not a leading voluntary donor to OHCHR, yet it specifically selected Saul’s mandate for a $150,000 earmarked contribution. The question is not whether China is permitted to contribute to the UN human rights system, but why it chose to fund this particular mandate rather than support the Special Procedures system generally.
Rebuttal: Saul emphatically asserted that China does not have “any control over the way that money is spent.” OHCHR similarly states that voluntary contributions are governed by “UN financial rules, policies and oversight mechanisms” that do not give donors “any role in the appointment, direction, priorities, findings or conclusions of mandate holders.”
However, the absence of formal donor control does not preclude indirect influence over a mandate-holder’s priorities and agenda.
A study published by the European Centre for Law and Justice (ECLJ), based on interviews with mandate-holders conducted between 2015 and 2019, documented concerns about the influence of voluntary funding on the work of UN human rights experts. The study quoted a former chair of the Coordination Committee of Special Procedures, who warned that donor funding could shape experts’ agendas. The report also noted that several experts described funding arrangements in which financial support was conditional upon undertaking specific projects related to their mandates (pp. 37–38).
These findings illustrate why compliance with UN financial rules does not, by itself, resolve concerns about the potential influence of earmarked funding.
Saul also asserted that China’s contribution “goes simply to funding the staff that support my mandate in Geneva and New York.” However, he provided no supporting documentation and the 2024 Facts & Figures Report does not establish how the $150,000 was ultimately spent. Even accepting his explanation, the use of the funds for staffing would not, in itself, resolve questions about the potential influence of earmarked funding on a mandate-holder’s priorities.
Rebuttal: Saul further claimed that he has “criticized China on many occasions,” citing his work on Xinjiang, Hong Kong’s National Security Law, and the prosecution of Jimmy Lai.
Yet his record is more limited than his broad assurances suggest. Saul has not dedicated a single report or country visit to China and has not issued a standalone public statement specifically addressing China’s treatment of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang. Although his 2025 General Assembly report briefly addressed the situation in Xinjiang, it did so within a broader thematic report on administrative counterterrorism measures.

articles.title_zh: Gaming Phones Are Finally As Obnoxious as Gaming PCs
articles.content_orig:
RedMagic Android Announcement
Back in mid-October, the RedMagic 12 Pro+ was unveiled in China , and RedMagic said at the time that it would also launch globally as the RedMagic 12 Pro. Today, the RedMagic 12 Pro is official for the rest of the world, and it keeps the RGB-lit liquid cooling and the 8,400 mAh battery of its Chinese counterpart.
That battery is 12% bigger than the 7,500 mAh cell in the RedMagic 11 Pro , yet the new handset is thinner, at 8.5mm (vs. 8.9mm). Charging is where the global model differs from the Chinese one - you get 80W wired charging instead of 120W, along with wireless and bypass charging.
The 6.85-inch 1.5K BOE-made X11 OLED screen has what the company says is the industry's first 185Hz refresh rate paired with a 'true full-screen' design with an under-display selfie camera. The panel comes with 0.96mm bezels, reaches 1,900 nits of global peak brightness and 5,000 nits of local peak brightness, and offers an instantaneous touch sampling rate of up to 5,000Hz. Hidden underneath are a ninth-generation 16MP selfie camera developed with BOE and a 3D ultrasonic fingerprint reader.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is at the helm, joined by the in-house RedCore R5 gaming chip and the G1 display chip, with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. On the back, there's a 50MP main camera with OIS and a 50MP ultrawide.
The RedMagic 12 Pro in Nightfreeze
The AquaCore Cooling System 3.0 combines the dual-loop liquid cooling, which now lights up in RGB, with a 25,500 RPM fan, a vapor chamber with a 15% larger effective cooling area, and Liquid Metal 4.0. The new micro-pump delivers up to 130kPa of output pressure, 85% more than its predecessor's, while drawing as little as 20mW.
The phone is IP68/IP69-rated for dust and water resistance, while the fan area carries a separate IPX8 rating. You also get 520Hz shoulder triggers (the Chinese model's are rated at 700Hz), stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, an X-axis linear motor, an IR blaster, NFC, Wi-Fi 7, and a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port. It runs RedMagic OS 12 based on Android 17, with Gemini integration, PC game emulation, and Steam access through the X-Gravity gaming center.
The RedMagic 12 Pro in Subzero
The RedMagic 12 Pro comes in Nightfreeze (transparent black) and Subzero (transparent silver) color options. Here's a handy table with pricing information for all possible versions.
For comparison, the RedMagic 11 Pro started at €699 last year, so every configuration is now €200 more expensive, and the top one also drops from 24GB to 16GB of RAM.
Early Bird vouchers will be sold from November 12 to 17, and voucher holders can place orders on November 17, getting a free 80W charger and a RedMagic-branded item. Open sales start on November 18 through RedMagic's official online stores and select retailers in North America, most of the EU, the UK, parts of Asia Pacific, the Middle East, Mexico, and Chile.

articles.title_orig: Sanctions-evading China-bound billions turn untraceable in Moscow
articles.title_zh: Sanctions-evading China-bound billions turn untraceable in Moscow
articles.content_orig:
Keep independent journalism alive
At the sprawling Sadovod market in southeast Moscow, among the 160 acres of clothing, jewelry and appliance booths, at least eight teams are spotted, working apart from the everyday hustle and bustle of the market.
Throughout a business day, these teams, known in confidential records as “departments,” receive a steady stream of customers, almost always carrying bags of various shapes and sizes.
And inside the bags are piles and piles of cash – Russian rubles. These departments, staffed by payment brokers, are a key intake point for one of the largest, and most secretive, cash-processing operations in the world.
Welcome to the industrial cash machine that is A7, the payments giant backed by the Russian state.
Between November 2024 and July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 tons of cash rubles, worth more than $14 billion, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and Russian independent media outlet Proekt has found.
For A7, ICIJ discovered, cash is king, the jet fuel for a firm now under scrutiny as a “shadow banking network” designed to evade Western sanctions at scale, according to US authorities.
On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned A7 as a “significant transnational criminal organization,” which “utilizes money laundering methodologies to fraudulently move vast sums of money in violation of sanctions and other laws in the jurisdictions in which it operates.”
But while Western governments and banks scramble to trace A7 money flows through the international financial system, ICIJ’s investigation reveals that the origins of the bulk of A7 transmissions are, in fact, untraceable.
According to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ, and people familiar with the matter, a huge portion of A7’s payments do not stem from conventional bank transfers by clients inside Russia, but literally from hundreds of tons of cash rubles.
Leaked internal records allowed ICIJ to identify that a handful of wholesale markets and other businesses around the Russian capital, including Sadovod, where much of the business is done in cash, made up a significant share of the cash A7 processed.
The records show that while the source of the cash is untraceable, its destination is not: Most of the cash is bound not for Western markets, but for China.
A7 did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
In public statements, A7 has strongly rejected the US allegations of wrongdoing, saying that it “employs a modern, multi-tiered compliance system” and that it was “established to ensure uninterrupted settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures.”
“All clients undergo screening to identify risks and prevent the servicing of individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” it continued.
Experts say the fact that cash drives A7 raises the specter of a money laundering operation limited only by the size of the market and A7’s capacity to physically handle the cash. As such, A7’s cash-based model presents not-previously-understood challenges both to the conventional banking system and to law enforcement.
“Cash is considered one of the highest risk methods of payment and store of value because it’s anonymous, it can travel across borders, and it doesn’t attach to any specific individual or company,” George Voloshin, an expert at ACAMS , a global training body for anti-financial crime, told ICIJ in an interview.
“The A7 network not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls,” Voloshin continued. The fact that A7 takes massive volumes of cash from Moscow’s wholesale markets suggests that the company “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime,” he said.
Voloshin added that international banks bear an additional burden of tracing payments emanating from A7. “The main risk is that [foreign] intermediary or beneficiary banks become complicit in [a] form of criminal activity that they know nothing about, because they don’t have any visibility into what’s happening in Russia where the money originates from.”
On its launch in late 2024, A7 touted itself as a sanctions-proof payments system, and has come under increasing scrutiny for its role as one of the Kremlin’s principal channels for laundering billions of dollars worth of payments out of Russia and into the global financial system, via a global network of shell companies, often with accounts at major international banks.
As part of its launch, A7 integrated into its business a hodgepodge of informal payment brokers at Moscow markets, including Sadovod, according to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ.
For A7, “Sadovod is simply a big client base – a big, aggregated pile of clients,” a person familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told ICIJ. “And that’s exactly what they go there for: the money and the profit.”
For years, this ecosystem of market brokers converted importers’ cash into conventional bank transfers or crypto, most often bound for China. This informal system was upended by Western sanctions, which barred Russian businesses from the SWIFT system, the international messaging network that allows banks to exchange transactions. The threat of US secondary sanctions – which target entities for doing business with sanctioned states or businesses – made Chinese banks more cautious when dealing with Russia.
The informal cash payment system at Moscow’s wholesale markets “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” Ilia Shumanov, managing partner of Russia-focused due diligence firm Tri-Trace Investigations, told ICIJ. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
Under A7’s new, supercharged system, a platoon of market brokers takes in the bags of cash brought by vendors and makes an initial count.
The brokers then stuff the rubles into numbered bags to be loaded, along with clients’ payment orders, into vans bound for an A7 processing office elsewhere in the Russian capital, according to leaked internal payment and cash management records.
A review of cash deposit and internal payment records shows that a small army of 50 or so A7 cashiers feeds the cash into a counting system where the amounts are verified; A7 enters the bag number, ruble amount and the client’s payment order into a bespoke payment management system, then trucks the cash on to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, the Russian state defense bank, a co-owner of the company. PSB puts it in a vault and credits A7 accounts.
PSB acknowledged ICIJ’s request for comment, but did not provide a response.
Records show that A7 then orders one of a network of shell companies registered outside Russia to make a payment on behalf of an A7 client to a beneficiary’s account, often a Chinese exporter, at another bank outside Russia – without any trace of the cash, or Russian origin, of the funds surfacing on the wire transfer or supporting documentation. The shell companies are advanced funds from A7 in Russia which pass through Kyrgyzstan on their way to the payee.
“The only bank that sees [where the funds come from] is Promsvyazbank,” Voloshin commented. “And the only company that sees everything is A7 itself.”
With A7’s role in sanctions evasion increasingly in the spotlight of Western authorities, understanding the source of A7 payments will become a central challenge for Western sanctions enforcers and international banks charged with know-your-customer (KYC) and other anti-money-laundering obligations.
The scale of A7’s cash intake is visible in a series of leaked documents reviewed by ICIJ, including a cash deposit ledger dated to shortly after the company’s launch in late 2024. Over a six-week period between November and December 2024, that ledger and other documents provide a running total of

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.
I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters .
My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.
In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.
Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.
iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums , the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple :
Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos
Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.
There are a ton of other great additions in iOS 27.2, which you can read about below:

articles.title_orig: China’s 22-Year Mangrove Restoration Drives Dramatic Rise in Coastal Bird Diversity
articles.title_zh: China’s 22-Year Mangrove Restoration Drives Dramatic Rise in Coastal Bird Diversity
articles.content_orig:
China has spent a quarter-century restoring its mangroves. A new study suggests the birds noticed.
Reporting in The Innovation , researchers at Ningbo University find that China’s mangrove area grew 166% between 1998 and 2020, from 10,617 to 28,194 hectares. Over the same 22 years, the number of bird species recorded along the coast rose from 148 to 397, and IUCN Red List threatened species from 11 to 21—a 91% rise.
The turnaround carries policy fingerprints: the 2000 China Wetland Protection Action Plan and the 2009 revision of the Marine Environmental Protection Law preceded the fastest growth phase, 2003 to 2008. Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao, and Guangxi supplied 88% of the national increase, and average vegetation cover climbed from 31% to 38%—quantity and quality rising together.
The harder question is whether such restoration restores ecosystem function, not just tree cover. Birds make a practical yardstick: they sit high in the food web, respond quickly to habitat quality and food supply, and are counted by legions of volunteers. The team paired long-term satellite records of mangrove extent and density with those coastal bird observations, then used a path model to trace how mangroves might reach birds.
That model describes a chain: policy and a warming climate expanded mangrove area; larger, denser forests improved marine conditions and reshaped phytoplankton communities; bird diversity rose in step. Mangrove area tracked both bird abundance and richness closely (R² = 0.70–0.76, p < 0.001). Phytoplankton showed the strongest direct effect on overall diversity and abundance, and mangrove area the strongest on species richness. Climate had no significant direct effect—only an indirect one, through mangrove growth.
The authors are explicit about limits. Bird records come largely from observation databases in which survey effort varies by place and year, so part of the rise may reflect more observers rather than more birds. And denser mangrove is not uniformly good news: shorebirds that feed on open mudflats, such as sandpipers and plovers, can lose foraging ground when forest spreads across tidal flats. Restoration, the authors argue, should aim at a whole coastal wetland—mudflat, shallow water, and forest edge—not simply more trees.
Its contribution is scale and mechanism: a national, 22-year accounting that links a specific policy to a high-trophic-level group through measured environmental pathways, rather than a single correlation. The authors see the approach as transferable to other coastal nations weighing restoration against conservation commitments.

articles.title_orig: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.title_zh: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.content_orig:
We've now ended our live coverage, read more on this in our news story
King Charles addresses the slave trade in a speech to Commonwealth leaders, saying the "shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror"
He was formally opening the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda
The powerful words from the King were careful and considered, and he spoke personally which will have landed with leaders - but he stopped short of a direct apology, our senior royal correspondent writes
The King also outlines what he describes as the "crisis of our time" , citing "brutal conflicts" facing the world, the "catastrophic reality" of climate change and the "dizzying speed" at which technology is transforming societies
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also at the summit, saying he is "open" to a formal apology from the UK over slavery, but said reparations were "not the right answer"
As part of talks with fellow leaders, Burnham is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of paying interest
The Commonwealth leaders' summit is held every two years and allows leaders and representatives of the 56 nations to discuss the future of the partnership
Edited by Matt Spivey, with senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph and political editor Chris Mason in Antigua
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
The King knew he couldn't give the audience exactly what they wanted today - which for many leaders would have been a straight apology for the transatlantic slave trade.
That will have disappointed many in the room but the King did speak with personal conviction and genuine sorrow.
These were the most extensive comments he has made on the UKâs role in the slave trade.
He was as candid as he could be in a role that a senior royal aide has described as "transcending politics" on this diplomatically delicate trip to the Caribbean
He is a constitutional monarch who is guided by the position of his government. That position may be shifting but for now it remains as no apology and no reparations.
The King was heard respectfully and warmly in the room by Commonwealth leaders and in the hours ahead we are likely to get reaction from them to the Kingâs words.
We're now bringing our live coverage to a close, you can read more in our news story.
Joe Coughlan Live reporter
The King met with various international representatives on Tuesday during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda
King Charles III today addressed Commonwealth leaders at a summit in which he called the slave trade the "most monstrous injustice" and a "shameful chapter" of history.
Speaking at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the monarch said the period "fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow" - but he did not offer a direct apology.
Britain's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade began in 1562, and by the 1730s it had become the world's biggest slave-trading nation. , external
The King spoke of the character and courage to overcome "monstrous injustice" to bring about an end to the international slave trade, in which he said the "the Royal Navy played such a leading role".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also attending the Chogm, which is held every two years, and is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries. The summit continues tomorrow.
Before our coverage comes to a close, we will bring you some analysis of the King's speech from our senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph.
Successive prime ministers have ruled out making reparations for the UK's part in the transatlantic trade of enslaved people.
Last week Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open "to calls for an apology" but called reparations "not the right answer".
He is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset".
This would aim to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of interest on their debts. The Aids Health Foundation charity warned that one in three Commonwealth countries are in debt distress.
Alongside plans for a debt reset for these countries, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also expected to allocate Â£40 million for infrastructure improvements in the Caribbean.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister has said.
Bond, a network for organisations working in international development, welcomed the plan and said: "Too many Commonwealth countries are losing vital public revenue to unsustainable debt repayments and tax abuse, while struggling to fund their own public services including healthcare, education and climate resilience."
Protests, like this one in 2017, have called for the UK to make reparations for its involvement in the slave trade
King Charles referred to the slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" during his Commonwealth speech.
Buckingham Palace has been clear that it is not the King's role to decide whether the UK makes reparations for its part in the transatlantic trade of enslaved people.
Britain's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade began in 1562, and by the 1730s it had become the world's biggest slave-trading nation. , external
Between 1500 and 1800, around 12-15 million people were captured in Africa and taken to the Americas where they were forced to work as slaves. It is estimated that over two million people died on the journey.
The British Parliament passed more than one hundred acts supporting and protecting the slave trade and, with royal support and backing, had assisted the development of growing the enslaved African population in the British colonies.
British enslavers profited from the buying and selling of enslaved Africans to work on plantations and that trade became bound to Britain's economy and society.
Eventually, Parliament abolished the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, before banning enslaved labour colonies in 1833.
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
The words, as ever from the King, were careful and considered. But he spoke personally and that will have landed in a room full of leaders - many of whom want more from the UK.
There was no direct apology or offer of reparations but there was a sense of sorrow and contrition from the King in his own words.
There was an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the brutality of the slave trade.
But there was also a sense from the King that the most powerful way forward is to look to the future and ensure the next generation of young people in the Commonwealth have the best opportunities made available to them.
âEvil need not have the last word,â the King said.
Joe Coughlan Live reporter
King Charles III has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history", adding that the period still casts a "shadow" over the Caribbean and wider Commonwealth.
Here's a recap of what he told the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting:
Concluding his speech, the King says he has only had time in this speech to mention "some of the ways" in which the Commonwealth is able to use its "unique advantage" to deliver tangible change.
Addressing the gathered leaders, he says the leadership of the Commonwealth is "in your hands".
"Each of you has the opportunity to make the greatest possible difference, I pray that over the coming days you will embrace this opportunity and commit yourselves to action," he says.
Above all, he says he trusts that each of the gathered leaders will commit to a Commonwealth in which "our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose".
He ends by saying that he hopes people can draw inspiration from "this remarkable family of nations" as he himself has "always done".

articles.title_orig: NATO’s New Defense Plan Would Mean Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.title_zh: NATO’s New Defense Plan Would Mean Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.content_orig:
Russian threats and US uncertainty pushed Europe toward France's arsenal. What Greece gains, what it owes, and what happens in a Greek-Turkish crisis
The year 2029 is emerging as a pivotal milestone for NATO, as the alliance prepares for the possibility of a military confrontation with Russia, U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to leave the White House, and Moscow is projected to have recovered a significant portion of its military capabilities.
For Europe, these converging developments raise a fundamental question: Can it guarantee its own security without taking American military support for granted?
Uncertainty over Washington’s future commitment to European security has intensified calls for greater European defense autonomy. The goal is to strengthen deterrence against Russia while preparing for the possibility of an attack on NATO’s eastern flank.
The 2029 deadline featured prominently at the alliance’s summits in The Hague in 2025 and Ankara in 2026 . The ambitious targets approved by NATO cover a broad range of military capabilities, from logistics and aerial refueling to long-range strikes, space operations and intelligence. Discussions launched in recent weeks have also introduced additional requirements.
Through its NATO Defense Planning Process (NDPP), the alliance determines which operations it must be capable of conducting simultaneously, what military capabilities are needed and how responsibilities should be distributed among member states. Greece has a significant role in these plans, with the northern port of Alexandroupolis serving as a key route for reinforcing NATO’s eastern flank.
The NDPP consists of five stages: establishing doctrine, identifying military requirements, assigning specific commitments to each ally, supporting implementation and assessing progress.
Several elements remain under negotiation. One issue is whether to reduce the requirement for 18 additional crisis-management brigades, freeing up more forces for the defense of allied territory in a potential high-intensity conflict.
The talks also cover drones, artificial intelligence and conventional capabilities that support nuclear deterrence.
The biggest challenge, however, remains the American military presence in Europe. Washington is pressing European allies to assume a greater share of the burden, but a reduction in U.S. forces could leave serious gaps in critical operational capabilities that would be difficult to replace quickly.
Europe’s defense industry must also ensure that it can produce enough weapons and equipment to sustain prolonged military operations. NATO’s commitment to raise defense spending to 5% of gross domestic product by 2035 does not guarantee that the alliance’s operational shortfalls will be resolved by 2029.
NATO’s approach to Russia was summarized in three words by Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, at the Warsaw Security Forum: “Block, Blunt, Break.”
Grynkewich stressed that a conflict with Russia is neither inevitable nor imminent, with deterrence remaining the preferred option.
If NATO were attacked, the first priority would be to halt the enemy’s advance, prevent the seizure of allied territory and, if necessary, strike Russian supply lines and command centers.
Deep strikes against a nuclear power such as Russia, however, carry the risk of escalation. This makes the early detection of Russian force buildups particularly important, including through satellites and unmanned aerial vehicles.
For now, Russian activity is being manifested primarily through sabotage, cyberattacks and espionage operations. The European Union is advancing a strategy known as “pursue and protect,” which combines efforts to dismantle hostile networks involved in hybrid threats with measures to safeguard critical infrastructure.
Against this backdrop, the appointment of Yuri Gorlach as Russia’s new ambassador to Athens has drawn particular attention. Gorlach previously served as Russia’s deputy permanent representative to NATO and headed the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Crisis Management Center.
His appointment has reinforced assessments that Moscow may be seeking to monitor NATO’s southeastern flank more systematically, with particular attention to allied military shipments passing through Greece.
“Moscow is likely seeking more systematic monitoring of NATO’s southeastern flank, with an emphasis on allied military transport through Greece,” a well-informed source told To BHMA .
Alexandroupolis is a major gateway for moving military equipment toward Eastern Europe. The port is also included in plans for a European “military Schengen area,” intended to reduce bureaucratic obstacles and improve critical transport infrastructure.
The port features on a list of strategic hubs alongside Antwerp, Bremerhaven, Gdansk-Gdynia, Narvik and Esbjerg.
Greece is also investing in space-based capabilities to strengthen its military readiness, with plans to acquire 16 additional satellites.
The planned system comprises one geostationary satellite for military communications, three telecommunications satellites, six electro-optical observation satellites, three satellites designed to collect intelligence from electronic emissions and three synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites. The radar satellites would allow military installations and movements to be monitored at night and through dense cloud cover.
Secure military communications are a particular priority. Greece plans to integrate the geostationary satellite, which will serve as an information hub, into C5ISRT-T, an integrated command, control, intelligence, surveillance and targeting system developed with Greek source code.
A source familiar with the program told TO BHMA that details about the systems’ operational readiness and activation schedules are not being made public for national security reasons.
The value of satellite capabilities lies in both the information they collect and the speed with which it can be transmitted and analyzed. Ideally, radar imagery, optical images and electronic signals would be combined and assessed using artificial intelligence, a process known as AI fusion.
Even an estimated seven-minute satellite pass over an area of military interest could prove valuable if the resulting data is processed in time. The capabilities are intended primarily to serve Greece’s national requirements while complementing its cooperation with NATO.
France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Spain and Poland already possess or are developing comparable capabilities. France and Germany are also working on mechanisms to share satellite data.
Protecting space-based assets is becoming increasingly important. On the day Russia invaded Ukraine, a cyberattack on the KA-SAT satellite network disrupted communications in Ukraine and other European countries.
There is also concern over Russian satellites approaching Western satellites in orbit.
Following the example of the United States, European countries are therefore seeking to establish satellite constellations consisting of multiple spacecraft. Such networks would help maintain communications and other critical services even if some satellites were disabled.
Greece is contributing to European efforts by hosting one of the two permanent ground stations for the European secure military communications program. The country is also preparing to inaugurate a Space Operations Command.
By 2029, NATO will face a critical test: whether it has managed to close its military capability gaps, not simply by acquiring more weapons, but by improving its ability to detect threats early and respond quickly.
The challenge extends beyond military spending. It involves ensuring that the alliance can sustain operations, protect its communications and intelligence networks, and coordinate its forces in a rapidly changing security environment.

Oops, something went wrong
Job openings and hiring changed little in September, the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed, as the "low hire, low fire" labor market continued.
There were 7.5 million job openings in September, from a revised 7.2 million a month earlier, the report showed. The hiring rate improved slightly to 3.4%, up from 3.3% in September.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Layoffs were also little changed at 1.6 million, with 1% of workers losing their jobs. Voluntary quits ticked up slightly to 3.4 million, and the rate of quits rose slightly to 2.1%, from 1.9% in August.
The latest data suggest a continuation of a long labor market trend of slow hiring, but minimal layoffs. A fuller look at the job market will be released on Friday, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its monthly payrolls report for October. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the US to have added 65,000 jobs last month.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: King Charles to Give ‘Unflinching’ Speech on UK’s Role in Slave Trade
articles.title_zh: King Charles to Give ‘Unflinching’ Speech on UK’s Role in Slave Trade
articles.content_orig:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.
There has been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the trave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also at the summit, has previously said he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but that financial reparations were "not the right answer".
While there was no direct apology, he did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.
He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."
He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."
King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."
The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.
The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

articles.title_zh: Job openings and hiring edged higher in September, but it's still a 'low hire, low fire' market
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Job openings and hiring changed little in September, the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed, as the "low hire, low fire" labor market continued.
There were 7.5 million job openings in September, from a revised 7.2 million a month earlier, the report showed. The hiring rate improved slightly to 3.4%, up from 3.3% in September.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Layoffs were also little changed at 1.6 million, with 1% of workers losing their jobs. Voluntary quits ticked up slightly to 3.4 million, and the rate of quits rose slightly to 2.1%, from 1.9% in August.
The latest data suggest a continuation of a long labor market trend of slow hiring, but minimal layoffs. A fuller look at the job market will be released on Friday, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its monthly payrolls report for October. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the US to have added 65,000 jobs last month.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: Micron: A $150 Billion AI Reckoning Is Coming (NASDAQ:MU)
articles.title_zh: Micron: A $150 Billion AI Reckoning Is Coming (NASDAQ:MU)
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Micron (NASDAQ: MU) has had a fantastic year, with the stock up over 200%.
The memory maker became the center of the next major bottleneck in artificial intelligence. As clusters of graphics processing units (GPUs) scaled to meet the needs of larger AI models, memory, which feeds data to the GPUs in various capacities, also came into high demand.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Memory prices soared, resulting in fantastic results for companies like Micron. Here's what $6,000 invested in the stock could be worth by 2029.
Micron is one of the largest makers of NAND flash memory and dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), both of which play different roles in feeding data to GPUs .
NAND is cheaper and offers high-capacity storage useful for holding the massive data sets that feed GPUs during training.
DRAM is high-speed memory that holds data only while powered. In AI systems, stacks of DRAM silicon are used to create high bandwidth memory (HBM), which sits next to GPUs and holds model parameters during training and inference.
Due to the massive demand for AI and, therefore, GPUs and data, Micron COO Manish Bhatia said on the company's most recent earnings call that "we really don't have line of sight to when supply and demand balances."
Memory companies are often viewed as cyclical because it's difficult to match supply with demand, which can result in a supply glut at some point in the cycle. In this super-charged cycle, many investors have wondered if things will be different.
Micron has secured 16 Strategic Customer Agreements, with deals running three to five years, an atypical development for memory companies.
As a result of all this, Micron's earnings are projected to soar. Micron recently completed its fiscal year 2026 (ending Aug. 26), reporting diluted earnings per share of over $74. For fiscal year 2027, Wall Street consensus estimates project Micron's earnings to surge to over $172 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence .
In fiscal 2029, the 10 Wall Street analysts who have submitted estimates to S&P Global expect Micron's earnings to exceed $212 per share. Valuing Micron on its current forward 12-month earnings of roughly $172, the stock trades at a 5.65x multiple.
If I simply carry that multiple forward, Micron should trade at $1,197 per share in 2028, based on its forward projected earnings for fiscal 2029. That implies roughly 23% upside, meaning a $6,000 investment would be worth $7,380.
Currently, the market largely still doesn't believe this cycle is different, which is why Micron, despite significantly higher earnings, trades at a mid-single-digit multiple.
Some on Wall Street believe the company deserves more credit. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria stated in a recent research note earlier this month that "investors are early in their journey of understanding Micron's value, and that journey will lead them to assigning a far higher multiple."
The growth in earnings has been staggering, given that Micron generated only $7.59 in diluted earnings per share in fiscal 2025. If it can maintain earnings in the high $100s or low $200s, then Luria is likely right and the stock will rerate.
A 10x forward earnings multiple would imply a $2,120 stock price based on the fiscal 2029 earnings estimate, suggesting more than double Micron's current price. In that case, a $6,000 investment would be worth roughly $12,940 in 2028.
Investors are right to be skeptical, because it's quite possible Micron and other memory makers are over-earning.
Recently, reports of a new memory chip from China that could fit more memory in a denser area spooked the market, as did reports from South Korea citing industry experts who believe heavy supply will enter the market in 2029.
So, it's tough to predict how sustainable Micron's earnings are. That's why I believe owning some Micron stock is fine right now, but investors won't want to go in too heavy on the stock, which could be very volatile, even long-term.

articles.title_orig: The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026
articles.title_zh: The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026
articles.content_orig:
The Collins English Dictionary announced its 2026 word of the year Tuesday morning, with judges opting for “mogging.”
For readers not fluent in youth culture: Mogging “might involve making [anyone] look inferior in terms of appearance, confidence or status — anything, really,” according to marketing consultant and copywriter Rachel Quin, who authored a Collins article announcing the winner.
According to Collins, the term originated in the bodybuilding community as a shortening of AMOG (“alpha male of the group”) and penetrated into the so-called manosphere , a collection of typically online male communities united by their beliefs about masculinity.
“Fast forward to 2026 and it’s everywhere,” Quin added. And, crucially for POLITICO’s purposes, it can be applied to literally any situation.
With that in mind, we looked back at five top political moggings in 2026 — the more brutal, the better.
One minute, Keir Starmer was British prime minister with a thumping Labour majority cheering his every move. The next, he was humiliated and ousted by a northern rival who had done little to hide his own leadership ambitions.
Starmer, of course, tried to block the Downing Street takeover by Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.
But once Burnham loyalists and grumpy ministers had quit Starmer’s government in droves, the prime minister bowed out this summer after just two years in office and Burnham — having manufactured, at the second attempt, an opportunity to enter parliament — waltzed into the top job unopposed.
Call it the textbook framemog.
Mozambique’s towering president, Daniel Chapo — who stands more than two meters tall — loomed over tiny Russian leader Vladimir Putin at a summit between African countries and Russia in Moscow last week.
Countries signed a summit declaration pledging to expand “cooperation in energy, minerals, and digital technology, establishing Russian industrial zones in Africa, and localizing production” — but the defining image of the summit was a photo of Chapo dwarfing Putin .
Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, real name Braden Peters, likely breathed a sigh of relief, having suffered the year’s other most notorious framemogging, at the hands of internet character ”ASU frat leader.”
In a classic case of nominative determinism, Jacob Rees-Mogg, former British government minister and current haunted pencil, pantsed American commentator Tucker Carlson in a discussion on the latter’s YouTube channel in October.
Rees-Mogg may not have expected to find himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler, but that’s what happened after Carlson questioned why Britain had even bothered entering World War II against Nazi Germany.
Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler,” adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing,” in a clip that went viral and catapulted the Brexit hard-liner back into the British public consciousness.
Donald Trump’s bid to clean out the iconic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was initially hampered by persistent pond scum.
After a money-spinning renovation in early summer, algae came back with a vengeance, turning the water green and murky, while the blue paint job began to peel off the pool bottom.
Rather than turn his ire toward the contractors, Trump blamed vandals for attacking the pool, and his Department of Justice attempted to prosecute people it accused of damaging the site. Judges, however, dropped or dismissed the criminal cases.
Trump returned to the theme Monday — right before America went to the polls for midterm elections in which the country is laser-focused on the surging cost of living and corruption — holding a rally in front of the pool and recounting all the issues he said he’d fixed with the pool, including “tremendous algae.”
In Hungary’s biggest aura battle ever , conservative challenger Péter Magyar defeated longtime nationalist leader Viktor Orbán, ending 16 years in power for the populist prime minister.
Magyar, a former MP for Orbán’s Fidesz party, dramatically broke ranks in 2024, releasing a tape of his ex-wife apparently incriminating members of Orbán’s inner circle in a corruption scandal when she was justice minister. For two years, he consistently attacked Fidesz and Orbán over graft while building a movement to take down the EU’s problem child.
Magyar ultimately led a big-tent campaign focusing on cost-of-living concerns and pro-EU messaging, which turned into a landslide election victory that left Trump and the Kremlin salty .

articles.title_zh: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
articles.content_orig:
